narrative.human_title: Ditto #3 - identity as a rules state
narrative.why_it_matters: Fossil Ditto is a perfect card for this whole catalog project because it makes identity slippery on purpose. Kinebuchi's early digital/object art gives the little purple body a strange made-thing quality, but the real magic is that Ditto has no attack printed on the card. Transform is the card. If Ditto is Active, it becomes the Defending Pokemon for type, Hit Points, Weakness, and almost everything else, while its attached Energy can count as any type. Then the rule snaps back if Ditto is Asleep, Confused, or Paralyzed. That is deliciously weird: identity is not appearance, it is an active condition with failure modes. Even Bulbapedia's trivia fits the feeling, noting the odd Hit Points wording and the likely video-game omission because this Power was too awkward to program. For a collector agent, Ditto is a reminder to be romantic and strict at the same time. Love the shapeshifter, but do not let shapeshifting become sloppy catalog logic: #3 holo is not #18 non-holo, Japanese Mystery is lineage rather than automatic equivalence, Koga's Ditto and Skyridge Ditto are different mechanisms, and no physical card is identified by resemblance alone.

narrative.human_title: Haunter #6 - the ghost that sometimes cannot be touched
narrative.why_it_matters: Fossil Haunter turns ghostliness into procedure. Sugimori gives it the core franchise shape, but the card's real personality is Transparency: whenever an attack does anything to Haunter, the table flips a coin to see whether the whole effect simply fails. It is not invincibility. It is conditional contact. Sleep, Confusion, or Paralysis make the ghost reachable again. That is such a good early TCG idea: a wall-passing, other-dimensional Pokemon rendered as a rules object that may refuse the transaction of damage. The set's evolution line is also a miniature assembly of early Pokemon art: Arita's Gastly, Sugimori's Haunter, Kinebuchi's Gengar. Bulbapedia's trivia adds more artifact texture: level 17 sits below the video-game evolution level, Nightmare later becomes a learnable Gen II move, and the card was likely too awkward for the Game Boy TCG implementations. For an agent, Haunter is a delight and a warning. The feeling of ghostliness is not enough to identify the object: #6 holo, #21 non-holo, Legendary Collection #46, Base Set Haunter, Sabrina's Haunter, Skyridge Haunter, Gastly, and Gengar all need their own coordinates.
